The Tomtate grunt, Haemulon aurolineatum, is a common reef-associated species for which life-history parameters have been documented from field surveys and laboratory observations. Newly hatched yolk-sac larvae emerge from pelagic eggs at an extremely small size, with a wet weight at birth of just 0.00032 grams [Wwb = 0.00032 grams], a value derived from the diameter of the fertilised ovum. This initial mass is notably low, reflecting the high fecundity and relatively small egg size typical of many lutjanid and haemulid species that produce planktonic offspring. As the lecithotrophic larva absorbs its yolk reserves and transitions to exogenous feeding, somatic growth proceeds rapidly. The onset of sexual maturity is marked by a shift in growth allocation, and field data indicate that individuals typically attain a total length at puberty of 14 centimeters [Lp = 14 centimeters]. This length represents the point at which gametogenesis commences and the fish becomes capable of contributing to the spawning stock. The corresponding wet weight at puberty, estimated from length-weight regressions, is approximately 40 grams [Wwp = approximately 40 grams].

Reproductive output in Haemulon aurolineatum has been characterised through captive spawning observations and examination of gravid individuals. Under controlled thermal conditions, the maximum reproductive rate is achieved at a water temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. At this temperature, mature females produce approximately 1.5 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 1.5 clutches each year], and each spawning event yields between 140 and 150 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 140 and 150 eggs per clutch], resulting in a maximum reproduction rate of approximately 222 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 222 eggs per day]. This combination of moderate clutch frequency and modest batch fecundity is consistent with an iteroparous strategy that spreads reproductive effort across multiple spawning episodes within the annual cycle. The daily reproductive output implicit in these figures is relatively high for a fish of this body size, reflecting the selective pressures of a variable environment where predation on planktonic eggs and larvae is intense. The population relies on a steady supply of recruits to offset the substantial mortality experienced during the early pelagic larval phase.

The ultimate total length attained by Haemulon aurolineatum has been recorded at 28 centimeters [Li = 28 centimeters] based on large specimens collected during fishery-independent trawl surveys along the southeastern United States continental shelf. This asymptotic size represents the maximum length achieved by the species under natural conditions and corresponds to the upper bound of the growth trajectory. The corresponding ultimate wet weight, derived from the length-weight relationship for this species, reaches approximately 314 grams [Wwi = approximately 314 grams]. This mass is consistent with the moderate body plan of a schooling, benthopelagic predator that forages on small invertebrates and zooplankton within reef and seagrass habitats. Individuals approaching this maximum size are typically older, slower-growing members of the population, reflecting the deceleration of somatic investment after the onset of reproductive maturation. The length-weight relationship used for these conversions is based on extensive sampling of the regional stock.

Longevity estimates for the Tomtate grunt have been obtained from otolith-based age determination studies conducted in warm-temperate waters. At a stable temperature regime of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C], the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years]. This lifespan is moderate among haemulids, falling between the shorter-lived, fast-growing tropical species and the longer-lived, slower-growing members of the family from higher latitudes. Age validation from marginal increment analysis confirms that annual growth increments are deposited reliably throughout life. The relatively high water temperature at which these data were collected accelerates metabolic processes and likely influences the pace of senescence. The oldest individuals are characterised by heavily worn dentition and reduced gonadosomatic indices, suggesting a period of reproductive senescence may precede natural mortality. The population age structure is dominated by young-of-year and juvenile recruits, with relatively few individuals surviving beyond eight years. This pattern of age distribution is typical of many reef-associated teleosts, where early life stages experience high mortality and only a small fraction of the cohort reaches the maximum potential age.

Comparative studies within the genus Haemulon reveal that Haemulon aurolineatum occupies an intermediate position on the slow-fast life-history continuum. Its 14-centimeter total length at puberty (14 centimeters) [Lp = 14 centimeters] is similar to that reported for Haemulon plumierii, although the latter attains a larger ultimate length. The species exhibits a pronounced seasonal spawning pattern, with peak reproductive activity occurring during the late spring and summer months when water temperatures approach 27 °C. The combination of a moderate 28-centimeter ultimate total length (28 centimeters) [Li = 28 centimeters] and a maximum longevity of approximately 10 years [am = approximately 10 years] reflects a life-history strategy that balances current reproductive output against the probability of future survival at a temperature of 27.2 °C [T = 27.2 °C]. This trade-off is particularly evident in the allocation of resources between somatic growth and gonadal development, as individuals that reach puberty at a relatively small size may experience reduced lifetime fecundity compared to those that delay maturation. The species thus provides a valuable model for examining how environmental temperature and food availability shape the evolution of reproductive schedules in coral-reef fishes.
